extracted.intended_audience: law students, journalists, publishers, lawyers, and others seeking an overview of U.S. defamation/libel/slander law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the substantive legal standards, defenses, and doctrines governing defamation (libel and slander) in the United States, with illustrative case law and statutory points. Useful as an evaluative checklist for whether speech is actionable and what defenses apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as an absolute defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is an absolute defense against defamation in the United States; meaning true statements cannot be defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states explicitly that "Truth is an absolute defense against defamation in the United States," and that the truth of the allegedly defamatory statement will always negate the claim (either because the plaintiff fails to prove falsity or because the defendant proves the statement true). Cited guidance: Digital Media Law Project. Practical note: proving truth defeats the claim regardless of other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual malice standard for public officials/figures (New York Times Co. v. Sullivan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officials (and later public figures) can only win a libel suit by proving 'actual malice' — knowledge that the information was false or publication with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origin: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964). The page quotes the exact definition: "knowledge that the information was false" or published "with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not." This standard was later extended to public figures. Practical implication: higher burden of proof for public-person plaintiffs; many follow-up cases refine what constitutes reckless disregard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different fault standards for private individuals (lower burden than actual malice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Private individuals are generally subject to a lower fault standard (often negligence) than public figures; states cannot impose strict liability because of First Amendment limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (1974) established that states cannot impose strict liability and suggested a mens rea/culpability requirement. The page notes that bloggers about private citizens on public matters may be sued only if negligent (Ninth Circuit / Obsidian example). Practical consequence: the required showing of fault depends on plaintiff's public-figure status and the forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion versus fact (opinion privilege limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of opinion are often not actionable, but opinion based on false facts, fact couched as opinion, or opinion that implies false facts is not protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains that while Gertz suggested opinions cannot be the basis of a defamation suit, Milkovich v. Lorain Journal Co. (1990) rejected an absolute First Amendment 'opinion privilege.' It gives the example: "It is my opinion that he is a liar." would not be treated differently from "He is a liar." Also warns: opinion that implies alleged facts or is based on false facts loses protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation per se categories (presumed damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of false statements are considered defamatory per se so damages are presumed and need not be proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per the article, statements are defamatory per se where they falsely impute one or more of: (1) injurious to another in their trade, business, or profession; (2) loathsome disease (historically leprosy, STDs; now may include mental illness); (3) unchastity (usually unmarried people/women historically); (4) criminal activity (sometimes only crimes of moral turpitude). Most states recognize these categories (except noted states). Practical note: per se status eliminates need to prove special damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody/obviously facetious statements not actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements so ridiculous or obviously facetious that no reasonable person would believe them are not actionable as defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Hustler Magazine v. Falwell (1988): a parody advertisement (false) could not support damages for emotional distress because it was so obviously ridiculous. The page notes later Supreme Court cases barred libel claims for statements that are so ridiculous as to be obviously facetious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 230 immunity for online intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: 47 U.S.C. § 230 generally immunizes providers and users of interactive computer services from being treated as the publisher or speaker of information provided by another information content provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains §230(c) prevents providers from being treated as publisher/speaker of third-party content and provides forums immunity even if providers are notified of defamatory material and neglect to remove it. Cases cited: Zeran v. America Online; Blumenthal v. Drudge; Barrett v. Rosenthal (California). Practical effect: website operators normally avoid liability for user posts; §230 was enacted in part to reverse Prodigy decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair comment, litigation privilege, and reporting defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileges that can lead to dismissal without trial include fair comment and criticism, the litigation privilege, and reporting/passing through information as general information or warnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes these privileges vary by state; the litigation privilege makes statements in litigation non-actionable; 'fair comment and criticism' reflects societal interest in commentary on matters of public interest (but Supreme Court has declined to hold it constitutionally required). Reporting/passing through information as a general warning can be a defense, and intent to defame must be proven. Citation needed notes appear in the article for some statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal defamation exists in some states (but not federally)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no federal criminal defamation/insult laws, but many states and territories retain criminal defamation/libel/slander statutes or allow criminal liability via case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists 23 states and two territories with criminal statutes (and examples such as Alabama, Florida, Idaho, etc.), explains that prosecutions are rare, and gives historical conviction/sentence statistics. It also notes some state statutes are limited in scope (e.g., linked to banking or hate crimes) and some jurisdictions have declared statutes unconstitutional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pollard v. Lyon five classes of oral slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral slander (slander) may be divided into five classes per Pollard v. Lyon: (1) imputing commission of a criminal offense involving moral turpitude; (2) imputing infection with a contagious disease; (3) imputing unfitness to perform duties of an office/employment or lack of integrity; (4) imputing prejudice in profession or trade; (5) defamatory words that occasion special damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pollard v. Lyon (1875) enumeration is given with explanatory parentheticals. Practical use: helps classify slander claims and determine actionability under older/common-law categories; modern statutes/cases vary by state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: falsity, fault, and damages (public concern and blogger context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs generally must prove falsity (except for per se statements), and public-figure/public-concern contexts often require proof of fault and actual damages; bloggers and nontraditional media may be subject to the same standards, but fault level can vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Obsidian Finance Group v. Cox (9th Cir.) holding that liability for a defamatory blog post on a matter of public concern cannot be imposed without proof of fault and actual damages. It also notes that bloggers saying libelous things about private citizens concerning public matters can only be sued if negligent. Practical point: plaintiff's status and the public importance of the statement shape whether falsity, fault, and damages must be proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPEECH Act and libel tourism (foreign judgments unenforceable unless First Amendment compliant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SPEECH Act prevents enforcement in U.S. courts of foreign libel judgments unless those judgments comply with U.S. First Amendment protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passed by the 111th Congress to stop 'libel tourism,' making foreign libel judgments unenforceable in U.S. courts unless consistent with U.S. free-speech standards. Practical import: plaintiffs cannot easily use foreign courts to obtain judgments that would violate U.S. speech protections and then enforce them here.

rubrics_metrics.name: No defamation claim for deceased persons
rubrics_metrics.description: In no state can a defamation claim be successfully maintained if the allegedly defamed person is deceased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states directly that 'In no state can a defamation claim be successfully maintained if the allegedly defamed person is deceased.' Practical implication: defamation suits typically die with the person; survivability of defamation claims is not available.
